Put an explicit human or policy decision at a pipeline boundary.

Some candidates should not continue on automation alone. An approval, review, or policy check may need to inspect the data after it is resolved, filtered, or reduced. This chapter pauses the pipeline at those deliberate boundaries so a decision can accept the candidate unchanged or block it before committed State changes.

Why this boundary matters

Stepwise belongs to the service-owned pipeline; the component presents the pending decision but does not control candidate transformation or State authority. It is more than a confirmation modal: an unresolved decision can pause execution indefinitely, so every application must provide a reliable path to continue or block the request.

Use this structure for

  • approval before publishing or committing a consequential change
  • confirmation after derived validation or policy review
  • staged onboarding where each boundary needs an explicit decision

By the end of this chapter

You will have Stepwise behaviors and a controller configured at Resolve, Filter, and Reducer boundaries, with explicit continue or block decisions that preserve committed State when a candidate is rejected.

Chapter 14 Starting Point and Boundary Decision

Start with the completed Chapter 13 project. This comparison lab updates configuration, service, component, template, and tests. It installs all three gates so you can inspect their different inputs; a production feature should normally choose the smallest number of gates that enforce its policy.

Choose the Gate by the Question
  • After Resolve: “May this normalized input enter domain filtering?”
  • After Filter: “May this eligible/refined candidate be reduced?”
  • After Reducer: “May this fully derived value become committed State?”
The Teaching UI Must Be Settled

This example uses native confirmation prompts and one-use decision contracts. Respond to every prompt before starting another request. The example does not implement timeout, navigation cancellation, durable approval, approver authorization, or audit history. A production workflow must settle pending decisions on confirm, cancel, timeout, teardown, and navigation, and must enforce consequential authorization on a trusted server.

One Decision Pattern at Three Boundaries
Gate Candidate shown Continue Block
Resolve Resolved input before normal filters Runs filters next Ends the attempt without changing committed State
Filter Filtered candidate before reducers Runs reducers next Ends the attempt without changing committed State
Reducer Fully derived candidate before commit Allows the attempt to proceed to commitment Ends the attempt without changing committed State

The checked-in component turns each pending Signal into a native confirmation prompt. The service consumes the matching decision object once, clears its pending flag, and then calls either continue() or block().

Step 51: Configure the Stepwise Pipeline
↑ top

Stepwise behaviors pause a pipeline candidate after Resolve, Filter, or Reducer processing and wait for one explicit policy decision. Register the three behaviors and the Stepwise Controller together in app.config.ts.

The controller is required because it carries each request to the decision source and resumes the pipeline only after you choose continue() or block(). A blocked candidate is discarded and the committed State remains intact.

Make the Change
  1. In app.config.ts, import withStepwiseResolveBehavior, withStepwiseFilterBehavior, withStepwiseReducerBehavior, and withStepwiseController from .
  2. Add the three behaviors after withArrayAppendMergeBehavior in the third provideFeatureCell() argument. Add withStepwiseController to the fourth argument.
  3. Reload, settle the hydration source, and confirm a Stepwise Resolve prompt appears before any Filter or Reducer prompt. If no prompt appears, verify that the controller is in the controller array, not the behavior array.
What to Look For
  • Stepwise behaviors decide whether a candidate may continue; they do not transform the candidate.
  • Only one Stepwise behavior belongs at each supported pipeline stage.
  • This teaching workflow starts no second request until the active prompt is settled. Do not infer a general request-serialization policy from that UI constraint.
  • The Hydrate Resolve and Reject buttons settle the asynchronous source; they are not Stepwise decisions. Resolving hydration produces a candidate that then opens the separate Stepwise continue/block prompts.
  • The Reset State button from the Lifecycle chapter demonstrates that lifecycle reset does not require accepting or blocking a Stepwise candidate.

Step 52: Configure Resolve in the Service and Component
↑ top

Configure withStepwiseResolve() in the service to place an approval boundary immediately after the candidate is resolved. The callback receives the current State, the resolved candidate, and a one-use decision contract. The service stores those values for the UI to inspect and waits for the component to choose a decision.

The component observes a pending Resolve request and displays a modal confirmation prompt. Choose to continue when the resolved candidate is acceptable; choose to reject when it should be discarded. Rejecting blocks the candidate and leaves committed State unchanged.

The Stepwise Resolve textarea shows the current and candidate values reported to the callback. This textarea is only to help visualize the data; it does not affect the decision flow.

Make the Change
  1. In example.service.ts, add the Resolve request interface, pending Signal, one-use decision holder, callback, and acceptStepwiseResolve() / cancelStepwiseResolve() methods shown below.
  2. Register withStepwiseResolve() before initialize() and publish the callback values without mutating them.
  3. In the component, observe the pending Signal once, open the confirmation prompt, and delegate exactly one accept or cancel action to the service.
  4. Resolve hydration, accept the Resolve gate, and confirm the candidate advances to the Filter gate. Repeat and cancel at Resolve to confirm committed State remains unchanged.
New Symbols at the Resolve Gate
  • StepwiseResolveRequest stores only the immutable current and candidate values shown by the UI.
  • #stepwiseResolveDecisions holds the one-use decision contract while isStepwiseResolvePending tells the component when to prompt.
  • #completeStepwiseResolve() clears the stored decision and pending flag before invoking continue() or block().
What to Look For
  • The service owns the Stepwise decision boundary, while the component owns the user interaction. The service exposes the callback data; the component turns that pending request into a confirmation prompt.
  • Accepting calls the one-use continuation and allows the resolved candidate to proceed through the pipeline. Rejecting blocks that candidate and preserves the last committed State.
  • The textarea is an observation surface, not part of the decision flow. It displays the exact current and candidate values supplied to the callback.
  • Stepwise Resolve pauses the pipeline indefinitely at a defined stage; it does not transform the candidate. The candidate continues unchanged only after an explicit decision.

Step 53: Configure Filter in the Service and Component
↑ top

Configure withStepwiseFilter() after the Filter stage. The callback receives the last committed State and the candidate after filtering. This gives you a policy boundary where you can inspect the filtered data before any Reducer runs.

The component uses the same decision flow for the filtered candidate. A modal prompts you to continue or reject the data after filtering and before reduction. Rejecting aborts the candidate without changing committed State.

The Stepwise Filter textarea displays the current and filtered candidate reported by the callback.

Apply the Resolve Pattern at Filter
  1. In example.service.ts, duplicate only the Resolve gate's request, pending Signal, decision holder, and callback; rename them with Filter and type the callback as filtered character input.
  2. Register this.#vault.withStepwiseFilter!({ stepwiseCallback: this.#captureStepwiseFilter }) after filters() and before reducers().
  3. Add acceptStepwiseFilter() and cancelStepwiseFilter() in the service and component. Observe the Filter pending Signal once and route the prompt to those methods.
  4. Continue at Resolve. At Filter, confirm the candidate no longer contains records whose last name is unknown. Continue to reach Reducer; repeat and block at Filter to confirm committed State is unchanged.
What to Look For
  • The service owns the Stepwise decision boundary, while the component owns the user interaction. The service exposes the callback data; the component turns that pending request into a confirmation prompt.
  • Accepting calls the one-use continuation and allows the filtered candidate to proceed through the pipeline. Rejecting blocks that candidate and preserves the last committed State.
  • The textarea is an observation surface, not part of the decision flow. It displays the exact current and candidate values supplied to the callback.
  • Stepwise Filter pauses the pipeline indefinitely at a defined stage; it does not transform the candidate. The candidate continues unchanged only after an explicit decision.
Focused Delta from Resolve

The storage and one-use completion pattern is unchanged. The meaningful differences are the registration point, the #captureStepwiseFilter callback, and the next stage: Continue now permits reducers to run. Use the final checkpoint in Step 55 for the complete file.

Step 54: Configure Reducer in the Service and Component
↑ top

Configure withStepwiseReducer() after the Reducer stage. The callback receives the fully reduced candidate, including its derived display values, before that candidate can become committed State.

The Reducer decision is the final approval boundary before commitment. The modal lets you accept the fully derived candidate or reject it. A rejection blocks the state update and preserves the last committed State.

The Stepwise Reducer textarea displays the reduced candidate reported by the callback, including the values produced by the configured reducers.

Apply the Resolve Pattern at Reducer
  1. Duplicate the gate pattern once more, rename it with Reducer, and expose stepwiseReducerRequest and isStepwiseReducerPending as read-only Signals.
  2. Register this.#vault.withStepwiseReducer!({ stepwiseCallback: this.#captureStepwiseReducer }) after reducers() and before initialize().
  3. Add the Reducer accept/cancel methods and one guarded component prompt, following the established one-use decision flow.
  4. Continue at Resolve and Filter. At Reducer, confirm the candidate has forceSensitiveDisplay and fullName and is sorted by last name. Continue to commit it; repeat and block at Reducer to retain the prior State.
What to Look For
  • The service owns the Stepwise decision boundary, while the component owns the user interaction. The service exposes the callback data; the component turns that pending request into a confirmation prompt.
  • Accepting calls the one-use continuation and allows the reduced candidate to proceed through the pipeline. Rejecting blocks that candidate and preserves the last committed State.
  • The textarea is an observation surface, not part of the decision flow. It displays the exact current and candidate values supplied to the callback.
  • Stepwise Reducer pauses the pipeline indefinitely at a defined stage; it does not transform the candidate. The candidate continues unchanged only after an explicit decision.
Focused Delta from Filter

Only the candidate timing and terminal Continue result change. Reducer sees the fully derived value, and Continue allows commitment rather than another domain stage. The Signal, decision-holder, prompt, and one-use cleanup pattern remain the same.

Step 55: Complete Stepwise Tutorial
↑ top

Your Stepwise example is complete when the controller and behaviors are registered in app.config.ts, the service pauses Resolve, Filter, and Reducer candidates, and the component supplies one explicit decision for each pending request.

What to Look For
  • continue() resumes the candidate at the paused stage.
  • block() aborts the candidate without replacing committed State.
  • The textareas show the isolated callback inputs so you can see exactly what each policy boundary evaluated.
Run and Verify
  1. Resolve hydration and continue through all three prompts. Confirm the reduced candidate becomes committed State only after the Reducer decision.
  2. Reload and block at Resolve, then repeat and block at Filter, then repeat and block at Reducer. In all three runs, confirm the prior committed State remains unchanged and no later prompt opens.
  3. After every run, confirm all pending flags are false. Do not start a second request while a native prompt is open in this teaching UI.
Production Extension: Settle Every Exit Path

This example does not implement timeout or cancellation on navigation and teardown. A production controller integration must settle its active decision when the user confirms, cancels, navigates away, the owning view is destroyed, or the approval deadline expires. Add those policies in application code before adopting this pattern; do not treat the native confirmation dialog as durable approval or authorization.
